mcqs.q: According to the AAE Glossary, an obturation technique fills and seals a cleaned and shaped root canal using:
opts: A root canal sealer together with a core filling material
A core filling material alone, compacted to the apical constriction
A root canal sealer alone, injected under pressure
A medicament dressing followed by a definitive coronal restoration
mcqs.explain: The AAE definition specifies BOTH a sealer and a core filling material — neither is used on its own.

mcqs.q: The material used to obturate the pulp space must be capable of completely preventing communication between:
opts: The oral cavity and the periapical tissue
The pulp chamber and the root canal orifices
The dentinal tubules and the cementum
The periodontal ligament and the alveolar bone
mcqs.explain: Obturation seals the pathway between the oral environment and the periapical tissues.

mcqs.q: The original endodontic triad consisted of debridement, thorough disinfection and obturation. What is said about the relative importance of these three?
opts: All aspects are equally important
Debridement outweighs the other two combined
Obturation is the single determinant of success
Disinfection matters only in necrotic cases
mcqs.explain: The triad is described with all aspects equally important.

mcqs.q: What must be ADDED to the classical endodontic triad for long-term success?
opts: The coronal restoration
A post and core
A second irrigation visit
Periodic apex locator readings
mcqs.explain: To the triad must be added the coronal restoration.

mcqs.q: In the root canal treatment triad, the stated purpose of ACCESS PREPARATION is to:
opts: Achieve straight line access to the apical terminus of the root canal
Remove all the smear layer from the canal wall
Create a reservoir for the irrigant
Establish a positive apical stop
mcqs.explain: Access preparation aims at straight line access to the apical terminus.

mcqs.q: In the same triad, obturation is defined by its purpose, which is to:
opts: Create a fluid tight seal along the length of the root canal
Sterilize the dentinal tubules
Reinforce the remaining root dentin
Permit periapical healing by inducing apexification
mcqs.explain: Obturation creates a fluid tight seal along the length of the canal.

mcqs.q: The aim of canal obturation is to fill the entire volume of the canal space in three dimensions. This explicitly includes:
opts: Patent accessory canals and multiple apical foramina
The periodontal ligament space adjacent to the apex
The pulp horns of the coronal chamber only
The resorptive lacunae of the external root surface
mcqs.explain: Three-dimensional filling includes patent accessory canals and multiple apical foramina.

mcqs.q: The AAE characterizes obturation as a 3D filling of the entire root canal system:
opts: As close to the apical constriction as possible
Exactly at the radiographic apex
0.5 mm beyond the major apical diameter
At the level of the cemento-dentinal junction of the coronal third
mcqs.explain: The filling is placed as close to the apical constriction as possible.

mcqs.q: The filling material used with a sealer should be biologically acceptable and:
opts: Semi-solid or solid
A freely flowable liquid
Water soluble
Resorbable within six months
mcqs.explain: Sealers are used in conjunction with a biologically acceptable semi-solid or solid obturating material.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the three primary functions of a root canal filling?
opts: To strengthen the root against vertical fracture
To prevent coronal leakage of bacteria and nutritional elements
To restrain the growth of surviving bacteria in the dentinal tubules
To stop the influx of periapical tissue fluid
mcqs.explain: Reinforcement of the root is not among the three stated functions; the filling seals, entombs and blocks fluid influx.

mcqs.q: An obturation that appears adequate on a single projection may still be defective. What does an ANGLED radiographic view characteristically reveal?
opts: Voids concealed by the first film
A second, untreated canal orifice
Overextension of sealer into the sinus
An external resorptive defect
mcqs.explain: The change of projection discloses voids that the straight-on film conceals.

mcqs.q: Most treatment failures related to deficiencies in obturation are:
opts: Long-term failures
Evident within the first post-operative week
Detected at the obturation appointment itself
Confined to teeth with vital pulps
mcqs.explain: Failures from obturation deficiencies are characteristically long-term.

mcqs.q: Why is damage from a deficient seal often NOT apparent in the short term?
opts: A low volume, or slow release, of irritant reaches the periradicular tissues
The periapical tissues are anaesthetised by the sealer
Radiographs cannot image the periapical region for six months
Bacteria are dormant until the temporary filling is replaced
mcqs.explain: It is the low volume or slow release of irritant that produces damage invisible in the short term.

mcqs.q: Compared with the apical and coronal seals, the lateral seal is:
opts: Not as critical, but still important in the inner middle aspect of the canal
Of greater importance than either
Entirely irrelevant once the apical seal is sound
Only relevant in immature teeth
mcqs.explain: The lateral seal is less critical than the apical and coronal seals, yet a seal in the inner middle aspect remains important.

mcqs.q: Lateral canals are of concern during obturation because they:
opts: Constitute a potential channel for irritants from the canal to the periodontium
Always contain a second apical foramen
Prevent the spreader from reaching working length
Are the usual site of instrument separation
mcqs.explain: They form a potential channel between the canal and the periodontium.

mcqs.q: Current best evidence on the healing of apical periodontitis indicates that the odds of healing increase with:
opts: Both adequate root canal treatment and adequate restorative treatment
Adequate root canal treatment regardless of the restoration
Adequate restorative treatment regardless of the canal filling
The use of a warm vertical rather than a lateral technique
mcqs.explain: The odds of healing rise with adequate endodontic AND adequate restorative treatment — which is why the coronal seal matters as much as the apical one.

mcqs.q: Obturation is described as a reflection of:
opts: The cleaning and shaping
The patient's systemic health
The choice of sealer
The operator's radiographic technique
mcqs.explain: Obturation reflects the quality of cleaning and shaping that preceded it.

mcqs.q: Which set lists the RADIOGRAPHIC criteria used to evaluate an obturation?
opts: Length, taper and density
Length, width and radiopacity
Taper, symmetry and angulation
Density, lamina dura and PDL width
mcqs.explain: Length, taper and density are the stated radiographic criteria.

mcqs.q: Beyond the radiographic criteria, evaluation of an obturation also considers the level of gutta-percha removal and:
opts: The coronal seal — an adequate provisional restoration
The pre-operative pulp vitality test result
The number of accessory cones used
The brand of sealer selected
mcqs.explain: An adequate provisional restoration providing the coronal seal is part of the evaluation.

mcqs.q: Traditionally, the apical point of termination was placed approximately:
opts: 1 mm from the radiographic apex
3 mm from the radiographic apex
At the radiographic apex itself
0.5 mm beyond the radiographic apex
mcqs.explain: Traditionally about 1 mm short of the radiographic apex, as determined radiographically.

mcqs.q: Kuttler described the apical anatomy as consisting of:
opts: The major diameter of the foramen and the minor diameter of the constriction
The apical delta and the accessory foramina
The cemento-dentinal junction and the apical third
A single uniform canal terminating at the anatomic apex
mcqs.explain: Kuttler noted the major diameter at the foramen and the minor diameter at the constriction.

mcqs.q: Following Kuttler's description, the apical point of termination is therefore:
opts: The apical constriction
The apical foramen
The anatomic apex
The radiographic apex
mcqs.explain: The termination is the apical constriction — the minor diameter.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed as a means of deciding where the apical constriction lies?
opts: Transillumination of the root surface
Tactile sensation at the apical constriction
Electronic apex locator readings
Apical bleeding onto the paper point
mcqs.explain: Knowledge of apical anatomy, tactile sensation, apex locators, radiographic interpretation and apical bleeding are the listed means.

mcqs.q: Prognosis studies consistently show that when obturating material has been EXTRUDED:
opts: Failures increase with time
Healing is accelerated by the foreign-body response
Outcomes are unchanged provided the material is inert
Failures appear immediately or not at all
mcqs.explain: Extrusion is consistently associated with failures that increase over time.

mcqs.q: Histologic studies of extruded obturating material showed:
opts: Increased inflammation with delayed or impaired healing
Rapid encapsulation and complete repair
Osteoid formation around the extruded mass
No measurable tissue response
mcqs.explain: Increased inflammation with delayed or impaired healing was demonstrated histologically.

mcqs.q: Patients in whom material has been extruded typically experience:
opts: More post-obturation discomfort
Less post-obturation discomfort because of the sealing effect
Discomfort only on percussion after six months
No change in post-operative symptoms
mcqs.explain: Overextension is associated with greater post-obturation discomfort.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the factors influencing the appropriate TIME to obturate?
opts: The radiopacity of the sealer selected
The patient's signs and symptoms
The status of the pulp and periradicular tissue
The degree of difficulty
mcqs.explain: Signs and symptoms, pulp/periradicular status, degree of difficulty and patient management are the stated factors.

mcqs.q: In a MULTI-ROOTED tooth, obturation should not begin until:
opts: The entire canal system has been cleaned and shaped
At least the largest canal has reached its optimal size
The tooth has been asymptomatic for two weeks
A post space has been planned in the widest canal
mcqs.explain: The entire canal system of a multi-rooted tooth must be cleaned and shaped first.

mcqs.q: A DISLODGED temporary filling at the obturation visit denotes:
opts: Leakage
Successful occlusal reduction
Adequate canal drying
Resolution of periapical inflammation
mcqs.explain: A dislodged temporary filling denotes leakage, so obturation should not proceed.

mcqs.q: The smear layer produced during cleaning and shaping is best described as:
opts: An amorphous irregular layer of organic pulpal material and inorganic dentinal debris
A crystalline deposit of calcium hydroxide
A biofilm of surviving anaerobic organisms
A band of predentin left by over-instrumentation
mcqs.explain: It is an amorphous irregular layer combining organic pulpal material with inorganic dentinal debris.

mcqs.q: The thickness of the smear layer is approximately:
opts: 1 to 5 μm
10 to 25 μm
50 to 100 μm
0.1 to 0.3 μm
mcqs.explain: The smear layer is superficial, 1 to 5 μm thick.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT given as a reason to remove the smear layer?
opts: It weakens the radicular dentin and predisposes to vertical fracture
It may interfere with the action of irrigants used as disinfectants
It may interfere with adhesion and penetration of sealers into the dentinal tubules
It may prevent gutta-percha penetration during thermoplastic techniques
mcqs.explain: Interference with irrigants, with sealer adhesion/penetration and with thermoplastic gutta-percha penetration are the stated reasons; dentin weakening is not.

mcqs.q: Removal of the smear layer after cleaning and shaping is generally accomplished by irrigating with:
opts: 17% disodium EDTA and 5.25% NaOCl
2% chlorhexidine and saline
10% citric acid alone
3% hydrogen peroxide and 17% EDTA
mcqs.explain: 17% disodium EDTA together with 5.25% sodium hypochlorite.

mcqs.q: In smear layer removal, the specific role of the CHELATOR is to:
opts: Remove the inorganic components, leaving the organic tissue for the hypochlorite to dissolve
Dissolve the organic components, leaving the mineral for the hypochlorite
Precipitate calcium onto the canal wall to occlude the tubules
Lower the surface tension so the hypochlorite penetrates laterally
mcqs.explain: Chelators remove the inorganic component; NaOCl then dissolves the organic remainder.

mcqs.q: Grossman's 1940 ideal requirements state that the obturating material should seal the canal:
opts: Laterally as well as apically
Apically only, since lateral seal is achieved by the sealer
Coronally only, since the apical third self-seals
At the cervical line and nowhere else
mcqs.explain: Grossman required a seal laterally as well as apically.

mcqs.q: Which of Grossman's requirements concerns DIMENSIONAL STABILITY?
opts: It should not shrink after being inserted
It should be impervious to moisture
It should be easily introduced into the canal
It should be bactericidal
mcqs.explain: Not shrinking after insertion is the dimensional-stability requirement.

mcqs.q: By weight, the LARGEST single component of a gutta-percha cone is:
opts: Zinc oxide
Gutta-percha
Radio-opacifiers
Plasticizers
mcqs.explain: Zinc oxide makes up about 65% — nearly two thirds of the cone.

mcqs.q: The approximate proportion of actual gutta-percha in a gutta-percha cone is:
mcqs.explain: Gutta-percha itself is only about 20%; zinc oxide is 65%.

mcqs.q: Radio-opacifiers and plasticizers make up what proportions of a gutta-percha cone?
opts: 10% and 5% respectively
5% and 10% respectively
15% and 15% respectively
2% and 8% respectively
mcqs.explain: 10% radio-opacifiers and 5% plasticizers, with 65% zinc oxide and 20% gutta-percha.

mcqs.q: Chemically, gutta-percha is:
opts: The trans isomer of polyisoprene
The cis isomer of polyisoprene
A polymerized methacrylate resin
A zinc oxide–eugenol complex
mcqs.explain: Gutta-percha is the trans isomer of polyisoprene (rubber).

mcqs.q: Which crystalline form is used in MOST gutta-percha cones, and why?
opts: The β-form, because it is less brittle
The α-form, because it is less brittle
The β-form, because it has better flow
The α-form, because it is more radiopaque
mcqs.explain: The β-form is used in most cones because it is less brittle than the α-form.

mcqs.q: The α-form of gutta-percha is preferred for INJECTABLE products because of its:
opts: Better flow characteristics
Greater rigidity
Higher zinc oxide content
Resistance to oxidation
mcqs.explain: The α-form is chosen for injectable products for its better flow.

mcqs.q: Standardized gutta-percha cones correspond in diameter and taper to shaping instruments under which standard, and at what taper?
opts: ISO 6877, with a 2% taper
ISO 3630, with a 4% taper
ISO 6877, with a 6% taper
ISO 1797, with a variable taper
mcqs.explain: Standardized cones follow ISO 6877 with a 2% taper.

mcqs.q: The size range of standardized gutta-percha cones is:
opts: ISO 10 to ISO 140
ISO 15 to ISO 80
ISO 6 to ISO 60
ISO 20 to ISO 100
mcqs.explain: Standardized cones range from ISO 10 to ISO 140.

mcqs.q: Greater taper cones are produced with tapers of:
opts: 4% or 6%, and up to 12%, or with varying taper
2% or 3% only
A fixed 10% in every size
mcqs.explain: Greater taper cones are 4% or 6% and up to 12%, or have varying taper.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes the sizing system of ACCESSORY cones?
opts: The tip of the cone has one size and the body another
They are sized only by length, not diameter
They use the same ISO numbers as files but double the taper
They are unsized and must be cut to fit
mcqs.explain: Accessory cones use a different system in which tip and body carry different sizes.

mcqs.q: A set of cones labelled 'extra fine, fine fine, fine, medium fine, fine medium, medium, large, extra large' describes:
opts: Accessory gutta-percha cones
Standardized gutta-percha cones
ProTaper greater taper cones
Silver cones
mcqs.explain: That naming series is the accessory (conventional) cone range.

mcqs.q: Three size #30 gutta-percha points exhibiting .02, .04 and .06 differ from one another in:
opts: Body taper, with the same tip diameter
Tip diameter, with the same body taper
Length, with identical taper and tip
Radiopacity, with identical geometry
mcqs.explain: They share the #30 tip diameter and differ in the taper of the body.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of gutta-percha?
opts: Lack of adhesion to dentin
Radiopacity
Minimal toxicity
Ease of manipulation
mcqs.explain: Lack of adhesion to dentin is a disadvantage; the other three are advantages.

mcqs.q: The slight elasticity of gutta-percha is a disadvantage because it causes:
opts: A rebound and pulling away from the canal walls
Irreversible plastic flow under occlusal load
Chemical breakdown of the sealer
Expansion that fractures thin roots
mcqs.explain: Its slight elasticity produces a rebound that pulls the material away from the canal walls.

mcqs.q: The PLASTICITY of gutta-percha is listed as an advantage because, when warmed:
opts: It can be packed with pluggers and its mass increases per given volume
It sets rigidly and resists displacement
It becomes radiolucent and reveals voids
It chemically bonds to the dentinal tubules
mcqs.explain: Warmed gutta-percha can be packed with pluggers, increasing mass per given volume.

mcqs.q: Warmed gutta-percha presents which particular drawback?
opts: It shrinks during cooling
It expands irreversibly on cooling
It loses all radiopacity above 60 °C
It becomes permanently soluble in tissue fluid
mcqs.explain: Warmed gutta-percha shrinks as it cools.

mcqs.q: Gutta-percha may be removed partially or totally. Partial removal is performed to allow:
opts: Post placement
Apexification
Intracanal medication
Periapical curettage
mcqs.explain: Partial removal allows post placement; total removal is for re-treatment.

mcqs.q: Chairside disinfection of a gutta-percha cone is performed by submersion for:
opts: 1 minute in 5.25% NaOCl, followed by rinsing in ethyl alcohol
10 minutes in 2% glutaraldehyde, followed by a water rinse
30 seconds in 17% EDTA, followed by air drying
5 minutes in 2% chlorhexidine, followed by saline
mcqs.explain: One minute in 5.25% NaOCl, then an ethyl alcohol rinse to remove NaOCl crystals.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of the ETHYL ALCOHOL rinse after hypochlorite disinfection of a cone?
opts: To remove NaOCl crystals from the cone surface
To sterilize spores the hypochlorite cannot kill
To soften the cone before it is seated
To increase the radiopacity of the cone
mcqs.explain: The alcohol rinse removes residual NaOCl crystals.

mcqs.q: Submersion in 5.25% sodium hypochlorite eliminates the spores of:
opts: Bacillus subtilis
Enterococcus faecalis
Candida albicans
Clostridium tetani
mcqs.explain: 5.25% NaOCl eliminates Bacillus subtilis spores.

mcqs.q: Gutta-percha becomes BRITTLE because it oxidizes:
opts: In air and when exposed to light
On contact with sealer
When stored below 4 °C
In the presence of moisture only
mcqs.explain: It oxidizes in air and on exposure to light, becoming brittle.

mcqs.q: The recommended storage that EXTENDS the shelf life of gutta-percha is:
opts: A refrigerator — a cool, dry place
A warming cabinet at 37 °C
Immersion in 70% alcohol
A sealed container of glycerine
mcqs.explain: A cool dry place; refrigeration extends the shelf life.

mcqs.q: The working end that is TAPERED and POINTED, intended to displace gutta-percha laterally, belongs to:
opts: A spreader
A plugger
A Hedström file
A Gates-Glidden drill
mcqs.explain: The spreader is tapered and pointed and displaces gutta-percha laterally.

mcqs.q: A plugger differs from a spreader in that its working end is:
opts: Blunt (flat)
Sharply pointed
Barbed
Non-cutting but spiralled
mcqs.explain: The plugger has a blunt, flat end, so it compacts vertically.

mcqs.q: During spreader fit, the rubber stop is set and the instrument should fit within:
opts: 1–2 mm of full working length
3–4 mm of full working length
Exactly at full working length
5 mm of the canal orifice
mcqs.explain: The spreader should fit within 1–2 mm of FWL.

mcqs.q: If the selected finger spreader will NOT fit within 1–2 mm of full working length, the correct interpretation is that:
opts: More shaping is required, because the apical size and taper are inadequate
The master cone must be downsized
The canal is over-prepared and a larger cone is needed
A different sealer should be chosen
mcqs.explain: Failure of the spreader to reach that depth means the apical size and taper are inadequate and more shaping is required.

mcqs.q: Spreader fit is also used as a check on:
opts: Satisfactory apical cleaning and shaping before obturation
The patency of lateral canals
The working length recorded by the apex locator
The seal of the temporary restoration
mcqs.explain: It confirms satisfactory apical cleaning and shaping before obturation begins.

mcqs.q: If the master apical file is size 30, the master cone selected should be:
opts: Size 30
Size 25, to allow room for the spreader
Size 35, to ensure tugback
Any size, provided it reaches working length
mcqs.explain: The master cone size corresponds to the MAF size.

mcqs.q: A master cone that shows resistance on removal is said to exhibit:
opts: Tugback
Rebound
Recapitulation
Patency
mcqs.explain: Tugback is resistance on removal, indicating a snug apical fit.

mcqs.q: With a correctly fitted master cone, the obturation length equals:
opts: The full working length
The full working length minus 1 mm
The radiographic apex
The spreader penetration depth
mcqs.explain: Obturation length = full working length.

mcqs.q: A master cone that will not seat to full working length may be obstructed by:
opts: Dentin filings packed in the canal
Excess sealer that has already set
An over-tapered apical third
Residual chlorhexidine precipitate at the orifice
mcqs.explain: Dentin filings sometimes prevent the cone from seating; reinserting the MAF clears them.

mcqs.q: When a master cone binds SHORT, which is NOT one of the three potential issues at work?
opts: The sealer has been mixed too thickly
The shape of the canal is improper for the cone chosen
The wrong cone has been chosen
Debris is packed in the canal
mcqs.explain: The three issues are canal shape, wrong cone and packed debris.

mcqs.q: In problem-solving a short master cone, recapitulation should be performed with:
opts: The last K-file used
A new file one size larger
A Gates-Glidden drill
A finger spreader
mcqs.explain: Recapitulation is performed with the last K-file.

mcqs.q: Enlarging a canal with NiTi ROTARY instruments often produces a canal that is:
opts: Larger than the instrument size
Smaller than the instrument size
Exactly the instrument size in every third
Round only in the coronal third
mcqs.explain: Rotary NiTi enlargement often yields a canal larger than the nominal instrument size — which is why a differently sized cone may need to be chosen and adapted by cutting.

mcqs.q: If the master cone is LONG, the two acceptable corrections are:
opts: Select the next biggest size of cone, or cut the gutta-percha tip
Shorten the working length, or accept the overextension
Use a smaller spreader, or add more sealer
Re-irrigate with EDTA, or place calcium hydroxide and recall
mcqs.explain: Either select the next biggest cone size and remeasure, or cut the gutta-percha tip to avoid overextension.

mcqs.q: Gutta-percha master cones are preferably cut with a sharp scalpel rather than scissors because scissors:
opts: Leave flanges on the cut cone
Overheat the cone tip
Cannot cut greater taper cones
Contaminate the cone with metal debris
mcqs.explain: The figure notes flanges on the scissor-cut cone; a sharp scalpel avoids such irregularities.

mcqs.q: After marking the master cone to full working length and seating it, the mark should correspond to:
opts: The reference point
The cervical line
The cemento-enamel junction on the lingual
The level of the rubber dam clamp
mcqs.explain: The mark should correspond to the reference point.

mcqs.q: Once the radiograph confirms the master cone has reached full working length, the immediate next step is to:
opts: Dry the canal
Place the first accessory cone
Mix the sealer and inject it with a spiral filler
Re-irrigate with 17% EDTA
mcqs.explain: The canal is dried, after which the tooth is ready to obturate.

mcqs.q: In the lateral compaction technique described, the sealer is carried into the canal on:
opts: The master apical file, coated with sealer
A lentulo spiral at low speed
The finger spreader
A paper point
mcqs.explain: The MAF file is coated with sealer and inserted to coat the canal walls.

mcqs.q: The master cone is placed in the canal with which motion?
opts: A watch-winding motion with apically directed pressure
A quarter-turn pull stroke
A balanced-force rotation
A straight push with no rotation
mcqs.explain: A watch-winding motion with pressure applied apically, until full working length.

mcqs.q: When the spreader has been inserted to resistance, it should be removed:
opts: With the same watch-winding motion
With a sharp straight pull
By rotating it a full turn clockwise
After waiting 30 seconds for the sealer to set
mcqs.explain: It is withdrawn with the same watch-winding motion so the space it created stays open.

mcqs.q: Spreader insertion to resistance should be done as quickly as possible in order to:
opts: Prevent voids
Avoid overheating the gutta-percha
Limit sealer extrusion past the apex
Reduce the patient's discomfort
mcqs.explain: Rapid insertion to resistance prevents voids.

mcqs.q: Immediately after withdrawing the spreader, the operator inserts:
opts: A pre-measured, sealer-coated medium-fine accessory cone
A warm plugger to compact vertically
A paper point to absorb excess sealer
A second master cone of the same size
mcqs.explain: A pre-measured and sealer-coated medium-fine accessory cone follows immediately.

mcqs.q: An accessory cone must be thinner and/or of smaller taper than the spreader so that it can:
opts: Reach the depth of penetration of the spreader
Be withdrawn again if the fit is poor
Avoid displacing the master cone apically
Be heat-softened by the next spreader insertion
mcqs.explain: The accessory cone must reach the spreader's depth of penetration, so it must be thinner and/or of smaller taper.

mcqs.q: The alternating cycle of spreader insertion and accessory cone placement is repeated until:
opts: The spreader can no longer penetrate beyond the cervical line
The canal is filled to the apical constriction
Ten accessory cones have been placed
Sealer is seen at the apical foramen on radiograph
mcqs.explain: The cycle continues until the canal is obturated to the cervical line and the spreader can no longer penetrate beyond it.

mcqs.q: The protruding gutta-percha points are severed at the canal orifice with:
opts: A hot instrument
A diamond bur at high speed
A sharp scalpel at the dam level
A rotary NiTi file in reverse
mcqs.explain: The protruding points are severed at the orifice with a hot instrument.

mcqs.q: If an obturation is satisfactory, excess gutta-percha is cut to the level of:
opts: The CEJ, bucco-lingually
The pulpal floor
The canal orifice minus 2 mm
The apical third of the chamber
mcqs.explain: Excess gutta-percha is cut to the CEJ level, bucco-lingually.

mcqs.q: If the obturation is NOT dense or voids are present, the correct action is to:
opts: Remove all the cones and redo the obturation
Add further accessory cones into the voids only
Place a warm plugger to collapse the voids
Seal it and review at six months
mcqs.explain: All cones are removed and the obturation process is redone.

mcqs.q: In a REAL PATIENT, when is the temporary restoration placed relative to the rubber dam?
opts: Before the rubber dam is removed
After the rubber dam is removed and the final radiograph taken
At the following appointment
Only if the patient is symptomatic
mcqs.explain: In a real patient the temporary restoration is placed before the dam is removed.

mcqs.q: Excessive apical compaction with a large spreader may result in:
opts: Root fracture
Sealer puddling in the pulp chamber
Loss of the apical constriction
Softening of the accessory cones
mcqs.explain: The radiograph shown demonstrates a root fracture from excessive apical compaction with a large spreader.

mcqs.q: The stated ADVANTAGES of lateral compaction are that it can be used in most clinical situations and that it:
opts: Provides length control during compaction
Fills canal irregularities better than any other technique
Requires no sealer
Eliminates the need for a coronal restoration
mcqs.explain: Length control during compaction is its other stated advantage.

mcqs.q: The principal DISADVANTAGE of lateral compaction is that it:
opts: May not fill canal irregularities as well as warm vertical or thermoplastic techniques
It cannot be used in canals with any appreciable apical curvature
It requires the α-form of gutta-percha rather than the β-form
It always extrudes sealer into the periapical tissues
mcqs.explain: It may not fill canal irregularities as well as warm vertical compaction or thermoplastic techniques.

mcqs.q: For lateral compaction, the canal must be tapered with:
opts: A definite apical stop
A patent apical foramen at least size 40
A parallel apical 3 mm
A step-back of at least 4 mm
mcqs.explain: The canal should be tapered with a definite apical stop.

mcqs.q: Accessory gutta-percha and resin-bonded accessory cones are chosen on the basis of:
opts: The size of the compacting instrument
The size of the master apical file
The radiographic working length
The brand of the master cone
mcqs.explain: They are chosen based on the size of the compacting instrument, and should be slightly smaller.

mcqs.q: The single-cone technique consists of:
opts: Matching a cone to the prepared canal
Compacting successive warm increments vertically
Injecting thermoplasticized gutta-percha without a cone
Cementing a silver cone with zinc phosphate
mcqs.explain: It matches a single cone to the prepared canal, cemented with a root canal sealer.

mcqs.q: The single-cone technique cannot be considered one that seals canals completely because, after preparation, root canals are:
opts: Seldom round throughout their length, except possibly for the apical 2 or 3 mm
Always oval in the apical third and round coronally
Wider than the largest cone any manufacturer supplies
Invariably blocked by a smear layer the sealer cannot wet
mcqs.explain: Canals are seldom round along their length except possibly the apical 2–3 mm, so at best only that portion is sealed.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as an ADVANTAGE of the single-cone technique?
opts: Good length control
Complete three-dimensional filling of irregularities
Independence from sealer
Superior resistance to coronal leakage
mcqs.explain: Simple, quick and with good length control are its stated advantages.

saqs.q: Define 'obturate' and 'obturation technique' as given in the AAE Glossary of Terms.
saqs.a: OBTURATE — to fill the shaped and debrided canal space with a temporary or permanent filling material. OBTURATION TECHNIQUE — the method used to fill and seal a cleaned and shaped canal using a SEALER and a CORE FILLING MATERIAL.

rows: to fill the shaped and debrided canal space with a temporary or permanent filling material
the method used to fill and seal a cleaned and shaped root canal using a root canal SEALER and a CORE FILLING MATERIAL

saqs.q: Name the three elements of the endodontic triad, state their relative importance, and name the fourth element that must be added.
saqs.a: DEBRIDEMENT, thorough DISINFECTION and OBTURATION — all three equally important. The fourth element is THE CORONAL RESTORATION.

list: DEBRIDEMENT
Thorough DISINFECTION
OBTURATION
All three equally important — and to these must be added THE CORONAL RESTORATION

saqs.q: List the three primary functions of a root canal filling.
saqs.a: Prevent coronal LEAKAGE of bacteria, bacterial elements and nutrients into the canal · RESTRAIN THE GROWTH of surviving bacteria in the tubules · STOP THE INFLUX of periapical tissue fluid and release of bacterial elements.

list: PREVENT LEAKAGE of bacterial organisms, bacterial elements and nutritional elements from the oral environment into the canal — coronal leakage
RESTRAIN THE GROWTH of any surviving bacteria in the dentinal tubules
STOP THE INFLUX of periapical tissue fluid and the release of bacterial elements

saqs.q: Why is the coronal seal as important as the apical seal?
saqs.a: Best evidence shows healing odds rise with BOTH adequate root canal treatment AND adequate restorative treatment. Coronal leakage reintroduces bacteria and nutrients, so a defective coronal seal causes long-term failure just as a defective apical seal does.

ans.text: Current best evidence shows the odds of healing apical periodontitis increase with BOTH adequate root canal treatment AND adequate restorative treatment. Leakage from the oral cavity reintroduces bacteria, bacterial elements and nutrients into the canal — so a defective coronal seal causes long-term failure just as a defective apical seal does.

saqs.q: Explain why most obturation-related failures are long-term rather than immediate.
saqs.a: A LOW VOLUME of irritant, or its SLOW RELEASE into the periradicular tissues, produces damage NOT APPARENT IN THE SHORT TERM; the injury accumulates gradually, so failure appears only at later review.

ans.text: A LOW VOLUME of irritant, or SLOW RELEASE of irritant into the periradicular tissues, produces damage that is NOT APPARENT IN THE SHORT TERM. The injury accumulates gradually, so the failure appears only at later review.

saqs.q: Why does the lateral seal matter, even though it is less critical than the apical and coronal seals?
saqs.a: LATERAL CANALS are often found in the inner middle aspect of the canal and are a potential channel for irritants to pass from canal to periodontium, so a seal there still matters.

ans.text: LATERAL CANALS are often found in the inner middle aspect of the canal. They are a potential channel for irritants to pass from the canal to the periodontium, so a seal in this region is still important.

saqs.q: Describe the apical anatomy according to Kuttler and state where obturation should terminate.
saqs.a: Kuttler: the apical anatomy is the MAJOR DIAMETER of the foramen and the MINOR DIAMETER of the constriction. Obturation terminates at the APICAL CONSTRICTION (minor diameter) — traditionally about 1 mm from the radiographic apex.

ans.text: The apical point of termination is therefore the APICAL CONSTRICTION — traditionally about 1 mm from the radiographic apex.

saqs.q: List the five means used to decide where the apical constriction lies.
saqs.a: Knowledge of APICAL ANATOMY · TACTILE SENSATION · APEX LOCATORS · RADIOGRAPHIC INTERPRETATION · APICAL BLEEDING.

list: Basic knowledge of APICAL ANATOMY
TACTILE SENSATION
APEX LOCATORS
RADIOGRAPHIC INTERPRETATION
APICAL BLEEDING

saqs.q: State three consequences of extruding obturating material beyond the apex.
saqs.a: Prognosis studies: FAILURES INCREASE WITH TIME. Histologic studies: INCREASED INFLAMMATION with DELAYED or IMPAIRED HEALING. Patients: MORE POST-OBTURATION DISCOMFORT.

head: Evidence
Consequence
rows: INCREASED INFLAMMATION, with delayed or impaired healing

saqs.q: List the four conditions that should be satisfied before a tooth is obturated.
saqs.a: Canal prepared to the OPTIMAL SIZE · in multi-rooted teeth the ENTIRE system cleaned and shaped · the tooth COMFORTABLE (no spontaneous pain, none on percussion) · the TEMPORARY FILLING INTACT — a dislodged filling denotes leakage.

list: The canal is prepared to the OPTIMAL SIZE
In multi-rooted teeth the ENTIRE canal system is cleaned and shaped
The tooth is COMFORTABLE — no spontaneous pain, no pain on percussion
The TEMPORARY FILLING IS INTACT — a dislodged filling denotes leakage

saqs.q: What is the smear layer, how thick is it, and why must it be removed before obturation?
saqs.a: An AMORPHOUS IRREGULAR layer of organic pulpal material and inorganic dentinal debris on the canal wall, 1–5 μm thick. Removed because it interferes with irrigants, with sealer adhesion and penetration into the tubules, and with gutta-percha penetration in thermoplastic techniques.

ans.text: An AMORPHOUS IRREGULAR layer of organic pulpal material and inorganic dentinal debris deposited on the canal wall during cleaning and shaping — superficial, 1–5 μm thick.

list: It may interfere with the action of IRRIGANTS used as disinfectants
It may interfere with the ADHESION AND PENETRATION OF SEALERS into the dentinal tubules
It may prevent GUTTA-PERCHA PENETRATION during thermoplastic techniques

saqs.q: Describe how the smear layer is removed and the role of each agent.
saqs.a: Irrigate with 17% DISODIUM EDTA and 5.25% NaOCl. The CHELATOR (EDTA) removes the INORGANIC component; the NaOCl then DISSOLVES the ORGANIC remainder.

head: Agent
Role
rows: removes the INORGANIC components, leaving the organic tissue behind

saqs.q: State four of Grossman's 1940 ideal requirements for an obturating material.
saqs.a: Easily introduced into the canal · seal LATERALLY as well as APICALLY · NOT SHRINK after insertion · IMPERVIOUS TO MOISTURE. (Also bactericidal, radiopaque, non-staining, non-irritating, sterile, removable.)

list: Easily introduced into the canal
Seal the canal LATERALLY as well as APICALLY
NOT SHRINK after being inserted
IMPERVIOUS TO MOISTURE

ans.text: Others — bactericidal or at least discouraging bacterial growth, radiopaque, non-staining, non-irritating to periapical tissue, sterile or easily sterilized, and removable if necessary.

saqs.q: Give the composition of a gutta-percha cone with the proportion of each component.
saqs.a: Zinc oxide 65% · gutta-percha 20% · radio-opacifiers 10% · plasticizers 5%.

saqs.q: Name the two crystalline forms of gutta-percha and state the clinical use of each, with the reason.
saqs.a: Gutta-percha is the TRANS isomer of polyisoprene, in α and β forms. β — most CONES, because it is LESS BRITTLE. α — INJECTABLE products, for BETTER FLOW.

ans.text: Gutta-percha is the TRANS isomer of polyisoprene and exists in two crystalline forms.

saqs.q: Distinguish standardized, greater taper and accessory gutta-percha cones.
saqs.a: STANDARDIZED — diameter and 2% taper matched to shaping instruments, ISO 6877, sizes 10–140. GREATER TAPER — 4% or 6% (up to 12%) or varying taper, for engine-driven instruments. ACCESSORY — a different system, the TIP one size and the BODY another, extra fine to extra large.

head: Cone
Sizing
rows: diameter and taper (2%) correspond to shaping instruments under ISO 6877; sizes ISO 10 to 140
4% or 6% taper (up to 12%), or varying taper — used with special engine-driven shaping instruments
a different sizing system — the TIP has one size and the BODY another; extra fine through extra large

saqs.q: List the advantages and disadvantages of gutta-percha as a core material.
saqs.a: ADVANTAGES — plasticity when warmed, ease of manipulation, minimal toxicity, radiopacity, easy removal with heat or solvents. DISADVANTAGES — no adhesion to dentin, lack of rigidity, slight elasticity causing rebound, and shrinkage of warmed gutta-percha on cooling.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Plasticity — when warmed it can be packed with pluggers, increasing mass per given volume
Slight elasticity — causes rebound and pulling away from the canal walls
Easily removed with heat or solvents — partially for post placement, totally for re-treatment

saqs.q: Describe the chairside disinfection of gutta-percha cones and state its proven effect.
saqs.a: Submerge 1 MINUTE in 5.25% NaOCl, then RINSE IN ETHYL ALCOHOL to remove NaOCl crystals. 5.25% NaOCl ELIMINATES Bacillus subtilis SPORES.

ans.text: Submersion for 1 MINUTE in a 5.25% NaOCl solution, followed by RINSING IN ETHYL ALCOHOL to remove NaOCl crystals. 5.25% sodium hypochlorite ELIMINATES Bacillus subtilis SPORES.

saqs.q: Why does gutta-percha become brittle, and how should it be stored?
saqs.a: It OXIDIZES in air and on exposure to light. Store in a COOL, DRY PLACE — a REFRIGERATOR extends shelf life.

ans.text: It OXIDIZES in air and on exposure to light. Store in a COOL, DRY PLACE — a REFRIGERATOR extends the shelf life.

saqs.q: Differentiate a spreader from a plugger.
saqs.a: SPREADER — TAPERED and POINTED, displaces gutta-percha LATERALLY to make room for accessory cones. PLUGGER — BLUNT (FLAT) end, compacts VERTICALLY rather than wedging laterally.

head: SPREADER
PLUGGER
rows: displaces gutta-percha LATERALLY, making room for additional accessory cones
compacts the material VERTICALLY rather than wedging it laterally

saqs.q: Describe the spreader fit check and state what a failure of this check means.
saqs.a: Set the rubber stop 1–2 mm short of FWL; the chosen finger spreader should FIT WITHIN 1–2 mm OF FWL. It confirms satisfactory apical cleaning and shaping and room for compaction. Failure means MORE SHAPING IS REQUIRED — the apical size and taper are inadequate.

ans.text: Set the rubber stop 1–2 mm short of full working length; the chosen finger spreader (e.g. medium fine) should FIT WITHIN 1–2 mm OF FWL. This confirms satisfactory apical cleaning and shaping, and that there is room for compaction.
If it will not reach that depth, MORE SHAPING IS REQUIRED — the apical size and taper are inadequate.

saqs.q: State the requirements for selecting and fitting the master cone.
saqs.a: Size must CORRESPOND TO THE MAF (MAF 30 → cone 30); DEFINITE APICAL RESISTANCE at full working length; TUGBACK on removal. OBTURATION LENGTH = FULL WORKING LENGTH.

list: Size must CORRESPOND TO THE MAF SIZE — e.g. MAF 30 → master cone 30
DEFINITE APICAL RESISTANCE when placed to full working length
It must exhibit TUGBACK — resistance on removal
OBTURATION LENGTH = FULL WORKING LENGTH

saqs.q: The master cone is SHORT of working length. Outline your management.
saqs.a: Recheck the cleaning and shaping. REINSERT THE MAF — dentin filings may prevent seating. Check the MAF reaches full working length and go through the hand filing procedure; the cone should then fit to the proper length.

steps: REINSERT THE MAF — dentin filings sometimes prevent the cone seating
Check the MAF reaches full working length, and go through the hand filing procedure
The selected master cone should then fit to the proper length

saqs.q: The master cone is LONG. Give the two options for correcting it.
saqs.a: (1) SELECT THE NEXT BIGGEST SIZE, measure to FWL and try it. (2) CUT THE GUTTA-PERCHA TIP — in either case to AVOID OVEREXTENSION. Cut with a sharp scalpel; scissors leave flanges.

list: SELECT THE NEXT BIGGEST SIZE of cone, measure it to full working length and try it in the canal
or CUT THE GUTTA-PERCHA TIP to correct the discrepancy

ans.text: In either case the aim is to AVOID OVEREXTENSION. Cutting is best done with a sharp scalpel — scissors leave flanges.

saqs.q: A master cone binds short of full working length. Name the three possible causes and the four problem-solving steps.
saqs.a: CAUSES — improper canal shape for the cone; the wrong cone; packed debris. STEPS — compare cone size and shape with the MAF; recapitulate with the last K-file; radiograph to verify working length; if still not snug, choose a different size and adapt by cutting (NiTi rotary often leaves a canal larger than the instrument).

list: The SHAPE OF THE CANAL is improper for the cone chosen
The WRONG CONE was chosen
DEBRIS is packed in the canal

steps: Check and compare cone size and shape with the master apical file
Take radiographs to verify the working length
If still not snug, choose a differently sized cone and adapt it by cutting — enlarging with NiTi rotary often produces a canal larger than the instrument size

saqs.q: Write out the lateral compaction sequence from sealer placement to the final radiograph.
saqs.a: Mix the sealer and coat the walls with the MAF · place the master cone with a watch-winding motion to FWL · advance the spreader and insert to resistance quickly · remove it with the same motion and immediately insert a sealer-coated accessory cone · repeat to the cervical line · radiograph · sever at the orifice with a hot instrument and cut to the CEJ · remove the dam and take the final radiograph.

steps: MIX THE SEALER; coat the MAF with sealer and insert it to coat the canal walls
Place the MASTER CONE with a WATCH-WINDING MOTION under apically directed pressure to full working length
ADVANCE THE SPREADER with the same motion and INSERT TO RESISTANCE — as quickly as possible, to prevent voids
REMOVE the spreader with the same watch-winding motion and IMMEDIATELY insert a pre-measured, sealer-coated medium-fine ACCESSORY CONE
REPEAT the alternating cycle until the canal is obturated to the CERVICAL LINE and the spreader can no longer penetrate beyond it
Take a radiograph and evaluate the fill
SEVER the protruding points at the orifice with a HOT INSTRUMENT and cut the excess to the CEJ level bucco-lingually
Remove the clamp and dam and TAKE THE FINAL RADIOGRAPH — in a real patient the temporary restoration goes in BEFORE the dam is removed

saqs.q: What do you do if the radiograph taken at the cervical line shows a fill that is not dense, or shows voids?
saqs.a: REMOVE ALL THE CONES AND REDO the obturation. The excess is only cut to the CEJ once the obturation is judged satisfactory.

ans.text: REMOVE ALL THE CONES AND REDO the obturation process. The excess is only cut to the CEJ once the obturation has been judged satisfactory.

saqs.q: Why must an accessory cone be thinner and/or of smaller taper than the spreader?
saqs.a: Because it MUST REACH THE DEPTH OF PENETRATION OF THE SPREADER. If as large as or larger than the spreader it binds before reaching the bottom of the space created, leaving a void.

ans.text: Because the accessory cone MUST REACH THE DEPTH OF PENETRATION OF THE SPREADER. If it is as large as or larger than the spreader it will bind before reaching the bottom of the space created, leaving a void.

saqs.q: State the advantages and disadvantages of lateral compaction, and the requirements the technique imposes.
saqs.a: ADVANTAGES — usable in most clinical situations; gives LENGTH CONTROL. DISADVANTAGE — may NOT FILL CANAL IRREGULARITIES as well as warm vertical or thermoplastic techniques. REQUIREMENTS — tugback at the prepared length; lateral space for the spreader; accessory cones slightly smaller than or equal to the spreader, chosen by the size of the compacting instrument.

head: Advantages
Disadvantage
rows: Can be used in most clinical situations
May NOT FILL CANAL IRREGULARITIES as well as warm vertical compaction or thermoplastic techniques

list: The cone must fit to the prepared length with snugness of fit, or TUGBACK
SPACE MUST EXIST LATERALLY to the cone for the spreader
ACCESSORY CONES slightly smaller than, or basically equal to, the SPREADER — chosen by the size of the compacting instrument

saqs.q: Describe the single-cone technique and evaluate it.
saqs.a: MATCHING A CONE TO THE PREPARED CANAL; the preparation is shaped so cone and canal match closely, and the snugly-fitting cone is CEMENTED with sealer. ADVANTAGES — simple, quick, good length control. DISADVANTAGE — cannot seal completely, since canals are SELDOM ROUND except possibly the apical 2–3 mm, so at best only that portion is sealed.

ans.text: It consists of MATCHING A CONE TO THE PREPARED CANAL — a type of preparation is advocated so cone size and preparation shape match closely, and when the cone fits the apical portion snugly it is CEMENTED IN PLACE with a root canal sealer.

head: Advantages
Disadvantage
rows: Cannot be considered a technique that seals canals completely — after preparation canals are SELDOM ROUND throughout their length except possibly the apical 2 or 3 mm, so at best only that portion is sealed

saqs.q: What is the danger of excessive apical compaction with a large spreader?
saqs.a: ROOT FRACTURE — the wedging force of an oversized spreader driven apically can split the root.

ans.text: ROOT FRACTURE. The wedging force of an oversized spreader driven apically can split the root, as demonstrated radiographically.

saqs.q: On what criteria is a completed obturation evaluated?
saqs.a: LENGTH, TAPER and DENSITY (the radiographic criteria), plus the LEVEL OF GUTTA-PERCHA REMOVAL and the CORONAL SEAL from an adequate provisional restoration. Obturation is a reflection of the cleaning and shaping that preceded it.

list: LENGTH
TAPER
DENSITY
The LEVEL OF GUTTA-PERCHA REMOVAL
The CORONAL SEAL — an adequate provisional restoration

ans.text: Obturation is a reflection of the cleaning and shaping that preceded it.
